pitch_detail.notes: Mostly high-quality, less-than-vertical rock, with some scrambling along ledges.
Slightly overhanging, easing toward vertical; includes the 3D Dike and a boulder-problem crux (about V7) on blank pinches.
Steep, three-dimensional climbing on underclings and jugs, with a key pinch through the roof.
Technical face climbing on excellent stone; the ledge at P10 takes a portaledge.
Overhanging for all four pitches, with boulder-problem cruxes (about V6 and V5); stick-clip some bolts.
Minimally cleaned mountain climbing; loose rock on the ledges near the top.

Where the lower ridge steepens into upper 5th class at a few trees, traverse left onto the more exposed side of the ridge. Find a snag beside a vertical #3-size crack. Climb cracks from the snag, including a short hand crack with 5.7 moves, to a belay just below the roof.

The 'Pac Man' pitch. Traverse out right under the roof, passing beneath its right side (going up and left over it is harder), and continue about 50 ft beyond. This pitch takes the most gear, and some parties find it the hardest. Above, scramble roughly ten minutes of class 3 up the ridge to the next steepening. The way on is not obvious here, and the gully alongside is loose.

Start on the steepening ground and follow cracks, belaying where comfortable or at the base of a 10-inch-wide crack. Parties often link pitches 3 to 5 into two. Some belay 20–30 ft past the fixed rap anchors for better stances.
Short start up the 10-inch crack, with gear in cracks to its left. Above it, follow finger and hand cracks past a shallow gully and some bushes to a belay on a flat section.

Either take the corner crack to the right or the cracks straight above to a tree, then lieback the corner the tree grows in. Above the corner, easier ground leads to the next steepening of the ridge. Much of this pitch is easier than the others.
Follow cracks up to lower-angle ground and belay below the final headwall, which has a #3-size crack out to the left. Pitches 6 and 7 are the best-regarded on the route.

Short, excellent leaning crack on the left that takes #3-size cams, only two or three pieces. The easier option is the blocky trough and gully to its right: walk a short ledge to an exposed step, then climb a second steep groove.

About 200–300 ft of class 3 along the crest, with an exposed 4th-class move near the summit. Topping out commits the party to descending the loose gully climber's right of the route. From the summit one rappel reaches that gully.

The first bolt blends into the rock and is hard to spot. Climb just above a left-trending overlap, then up past three bolts on thin, exciting face climbing to the anchor. Short runouts, and some poor rock between bolts.

Climb past two bolts to reach a crack. At the third bolt, traverse right and follow easier cracks to the anchor. Pitches 1 and 2 can each be rappelled with a 70 m rope. Short runouts and some poor rock.
The long bolted pitch. A hard start for about the first 20 ft, then moderate 5.7–5.8 face and slab climbing to a tree anchor. Inspect the webbing at the tree before trusting it.
Enjoyable cracks graded 5.6–5.7 lead to the top. Belay from a gear anchor or a tree. To descend, scramble back to the top of pitch 3 and rappel the route.

Scramble up dirty ledges until the first bolt shows on the cleanest black-and-white granite, then follow bolts up the slab into a chute between two stands of trees. Exit right, then shift the belay uphill and left to sit beneath a right-facing corner.
Stem the brown right-facing corner up to a roof; the crux moves here are exposed but well protected. Above the roof step right onto a short bolted slab. Bolts plus a few optional small cams or nuts.

The only fully bolted pitch: steep, thoughtful corner climbing on white marbled rock through two roof sections, finishing on a sustained arête face. A #1 or #2 cam is optional near the top. Stated length for this pitch varies between roughly 30 and 40 m.

Follow the corner ramp as it trends right and steepens into an open book, mixing bolts and gear. A variation traverses out to a slung horn for more exposure; either way ends at the belay below the final arête.
Three bolts up a short, fun arête to the top anchor. Leave a #1 cam in the overhang section to protect the follower. The double-rope rappel starts from a tree anchor above this belay.
Steep, exposed bolted face starting on slightly funky rock (yellow/orange lichen) that improves by the third bolt, building to a V6 boulder-problem finish.
Sustained climbing around an orange dyke with blind reaches and heel hooks through a horizontal roof; engagement stays high the whole pitch.
A relative break: hand crack and arete climbing, awkward for shorter climbers but easier than its neighbors.
The 'money pitch': a beautiful 45-ft finger crack to a jug-flake rest, then small feet and crimps into a V9/V10 boulder problem before a final mantel. The route's technical crux.
Slab rambling opens into a massive corner/roof feature with good offwidth protection and holds.
Short 4th-class approach into funky jams on a large flake, protected with small cams.
Ledgy, loose terrain finishing on an easier layback corner.
Overhanging chimney climbed by stemming and jamming; watch for a wedged block hazard.
Wide stems onto an arete transition into easy, enjoyable face climbing.
Loose blocks near an arete lead to the top; most parties rappel the route on a single 80m rope rather than continuing to the true summit.

Low-angle, sometimes water-polished slab at 5.4-5.8, with runouts that can be long but on easy ground; P7 climbs a short 5.7 wall before easing back. Competent parties often simul-climb the first six pitches. The whole route follows a gully slab, so anything knocked off above funnels straight down these pitches — the many bent hangers show it; do not linger below other parties.
A fun blocky ramp cutting through the steeper wall above the lower slabs. Protection is sparse — a bolt about halfway and a fixed pin about 15 ft below the belay — but the climbing is easy.
The first 5.9 pitch, on steeper rock where the bolts are closer together as the moves get harder. It ends on a large ledge.
Easy climbing above the ledge. Bypass the chain anchors and scramble up to the base of the steep wall on the left, belaying on a flake below the bolt line of the next pitch.
The first 5.10 pitch: well-bolted, balancy face climbing that is a fair test for the upper crux. Stay on the bolt line; forcing moves off it makes the pitch harder.
A more moderate pitch up to chains. The top of this pitch makes a worthwhile objective on its own; above it the rock and climbing are poorer.

Easy (about 5.0-5.8) but the most runout section, on fair, slightly polished rock that sheds stones onto parties below; P15's two bolts are easy to miss and P16-17 have only the stations. Where the wall kicks back, go left to a bolt, up and right to a belay between a stand of trees and a heather patch, then right along an obvious ramp to the headwall. Parties most often get lost here.
The first pitch of the upper headwall, where the bolt line picks back up, finishing on a tricky friction slab.

The crux: a steep, sustained wall nearly a full 60 m rope length, needing around 17 draws (bring long ones or back-clean). Its anchor has no chains; a chained station about 10 m higher lets two 60 m ropes reach the base of this pitch on the descent.
A chimney climbed by stemming and scrounging; it is often wet and can feel harder than the crux late in the day. Grades given for it range from 5.9 to 5.10a.
An easier, fun pitch up blocky ground, ending about 30 m below the summit.
A steep friction finish to the summit that looks easy from the belay but has few holds; well bolted and airy. Grades given for it range from 5.9 to 5.10a.
